title: Online Tutoring
summary: Learn to tutor effectively online: setting up your tools and connection, planning and running sessions, keeping learners engaged, tracking progress, safeguarding and professionalism, and running a tutoring business.
audience: Teachers, university students, subject experts and anyone who wants to tutor online

body.p: Online tutoring connects tutors and learners through video calls, chat and shared digital workspaces. It lets learners get expert help regardless of location and gives tutors flexible work. Good preparation prevents most technical problems.

list: A reliable device (laptop preferred; a phone can work for some subjects) and a backup plan if power or internet fails.
A headset with a microphone for clear audio; audio quality matters more than video quality.
A quiet, well-lit space with a neutral background.
Tools: a video-call platform, a shared whiteboard, and a way to share documents and record notes.
For maths and science, a graphics tablet or a phone camera pointed at paper helps show working.

body.p: Video calls use a lot of data. If a call uses about 0.5 GB an hour, 15 hours a week for 4 weeks uses about 30 GB. Turning video off when not needed, using audio with a shared whiteboard, and agreeing a fallback (such as a phone call) keep sessions running on weaker connections.

body.tip: Test your microphone, camera, screen sharing and whiteboard with a friend before your first paid session.

body.p: Learners value tutors who are organised and make every minute count. A clear structure helps.

steps: 5 minutes: greet, check how the learner is doing and agree the goal.
10 minutes: quick review and a few retrieval questions on previous work.
30 minutes: teach or work through the new material, with the learner doing as much of the thinking as possible.
10 minutes: independent practice while you observe and give feedback.
5 minutes: summarise, set short follow-up tasks and confirm the next session.

list: Ask for the learner's syllabus, recent tests and specific difficulties before the first session.
Keep brief session notes: what was covered, errors seen and next steps.
Send a short summary to the learner (and parents, for younger learners) after each session.

body.tip: End every session by asking the learner to explain the main idea in their own words; it shows what actually stuck.

body.p: Online, attention drifts easily and silence is hard to read. Active learning keeps learners thinking.

list: Ask the learner to do, not just watch: solve on the shared whiteboard, explain steps aloud, annotate a text.
Use frequent questions, waiting a few seconds for answers.
Vary activities every 10 to 15 minutes.
Use the learner's interests and real-life examples.
Praise effort and specific progress.
Check understanding with questions that require reasoning, not yes or no.

body.p: Small groups of 3 to 5 learners can be effective and affordable. Use breakout rooms or turn-taking, call on learners by name, and give each a role. Pricing per learner can fall while the tutor's hourly earnings rise: 4 learners at R120 each bring R480 an hour.

body.tip: If a learner goes quiet, ask them to show their working on screen; confusion is easier to see than to hear.

body.p: Learners and parents want to see progress. Measure it deliberately rather than relying on impressions.

list: Start with a diagnostic task to find strengths and gaps.
Set clear goals linked to the syllabus and the learner's exams.
Use short quizzes, past-paper questions and timed practice.
Track results over time in a simple spreadsheet or report.
Give specific feedback: what was good, what to fix and how.

body.p: Teach exam technique alongside content: reading questions carefully, allocating time by marks, showing working and checking answers. Work through past papers under timed conditions as exams approach, and review errors carefully.

Share progress with learners regularly. Showing a learner that their quiz scores rose from 45% to 70% over six weeks builds confidence and motivation more than general praise, and gives parents clear evidence of value.

body.tip: Keep a list of each learner's repeated errors and revisit them until they disappear.

body.p: Tutors often work one-to-one with young people, so safeguarding and professional boundaries are essential.

list: For learners under 18, agree arrangements with parents or guardians and communicate through approved channels.
Use professional platforms rather than private messaging apps where possible; keep communication about learning.
Never ask for personal photos or share inappropriate content; keep conversations respectful.
Record sessions only with consent and according to platform rules and data-protection laws.
Know how to report concerns about a child's safety to the right authorities.
Be punctual and prepared; cancel with notice.
Be honest about your expertise and qualifications.
Respect academic integrity: support learning, do not complete graded assignments for learners.
Protect learners' personal data.

body.tip: Write a simple policy covering communication, cancellations, recordings and privacy, and share it with families before starting.

body.p: Many tutors work independently or through platforms. Treat it as a small business.

Research local rates for your subject and level. At R250 an hour for 15 hours a week, 4 weeks a month, gross income is 250 x 15 x 4 = R15 000. If a platform takes a 20% commission, you receive R12 000, before data, equipment and tax. Set clear payment terms, such as paying in advance for packages of sessions.

list: Start with referrals from schools, friends and satisfied families.
Create a simple profile showing subjects, levels, results and testimonials (with permission).
Offer a short trial session.
Share free helpful content (tips, short videos) to build trust.
Specialise: tutors known for one exam or subject are easier to recommend.

body.p: Keep records of income and expenses, and register and pay tax as your country requires. Plan for quieter periods, such as holidays, by saving during busy exam seasons.

body.tip: Ask satisfied families for referrals at the moment they share good results; that is when they are most willing.
